lines.text: Day five at Uber. Data is clean. I know what every column means. Time to actually look at the thing.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: First chart I pulled — ticket volume by week. And right there in January — it doubles.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Clean as a whistle. The chart was honest. The number was real.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: So I'm typing into the recommendation deck — 'hire fewer agents, cut support costs, done.'
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: I'm one paragraph from finishing it.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: And Marco — my mentor — walks past my desk. Looks at the chart. Looks at me. And goes —
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Why did tickets double?
lines.speaker: marco

lines.text: And I'm like… I don't actually know.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: He hands me a marker. We walk to the whiteboard. He writes the question at the top. And we go.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: First why — why did total tickets double?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: I pull the data by ticket type. And it's not all of them — it's specifically cancellation tickets that doubled. Everything else stayed flat.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Second why — why did cancellations spike?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: I line it up against our release calendar. The jump starts the exact week we shipped the new rider app in December.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Third why — why does a UI change cause people to call support to cancel?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: I open the new app. Try to cancel a trip. The Cancel button — used to be on the home screen — is now buried two screens deep.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Riders couldn't find it. So they did the next thing. They called us.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Fourth why — why didn't anyone catch this before launch?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Pull the test they ran before launch. Half the riders got the new flow, half got the old one — then compared the two. That kind of side-by-side test has a name — it's called an A/B test. What did they measure? One thing — did people still book trips at the same rate. Yes, they did.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: They never measured what happened *after* the tap.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Fifth why — why was that the only thing they measured?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Because nobody on the product team was watching how many calls support was getting. Every product team tracks a little set of numbers each week — call it their scorecard. Call volume wasn't on this one.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Nobody on the product side was looking.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: And right there — at the bottom of the chain — the project changed.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: The recommendation wasn't 'hire fewer agents' anymore.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: It was — fix the Cancel button. Move it back where people can find it. And add support call volume to the scorecard — the numbers the product team watches every week.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Same problem. Different fix. And way bigger payoff — you're not just handling calls faster, you're stopping them from happening at all.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: By the way — this technique has a name.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Root cause analysis. RCA. Five-why is just the simplest version of it.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Same move works on almost any 'why is this happening' question. Customers leaving. A system breaking. A bug showing up. Most of life, honestly.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: The skill is — don't stop at the first answer. Keep asking why until something *actionable* shows up.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: So — you're about to get a number. Tickets up. Refunds up. Support costs up. Something like that.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: First instinct will be to recommend cutting it. Don't.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Get past the symptom. Find the why. The real project is always one or two whys deeper than where you start.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Alright — your turn. Here's the situation.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: A fintech app's password reset support tickets doubled last month. That's all you know.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Ask the first why. Whatever feels natural. I'll hand back an answer. Then you go deeper — five rungs.
lines.speaker: avery
